title: Indian Startup GalaxEye Launches World's First Optical-SAR Satellite Payload Aboard SpaceX
excerpt: The Bengaluru-based space tech startup's OptoSAR payload combines optical and radar imaging in a single sensor, a global first that could reshape Earth observation.
body:
• GalaxEye, a Bengaluru-based startup, launched the world's first combined optical and synthetic aperture radar payload aboard a SpaceX Transporter mission.
  • The OptoSAR technology fuses optical and radar imaging in a single sensor, enabling all-weather, day-and-night Earth observation.
  • Founded by IIT Madras graduates, the company has raised over $7 million and counts defense and agricultural clients among its early customers.
  • The launch marks another milestone for India's rapidly growing private space sector following Skyroot's orbital success.

A Global First From Bengaluru

Indian space tech startup GalaxEye has achieved a world first: the successful launch of a payload that combines optical and synthetic aperture radar imaging into a single sensor. The OptoSAR payload rode to orbit aboard a SpaceX Transporter rideshare mission, marking a breakthrough for India's burgeoning private space industry.

Traditional Earth observation satellites use either optical cameras, which fail in cloud cover and darkness, or radar systems, which penetrate clouds but produce lower-resolution imagery. GalaxEye's technology fuses both into one sensor, delivering high-resolution, all-weather, day-and-night imaging from a single platform — something no other company or space agency has achieved commercially.

From IIT Madras to Orbit

GalaxEye was founded by a group of IIT Madras graduates who began developing multi-sensor fusion technology as a college project. The company has since raised over $7 million in funding and built relationships with defense and agricultural sector clients who need reliable Earth observation data regardless of weather conditions.

"Military planners need imagery that works in monsoon conditions, at night, and through deliberate concealment — exactly the scenarios where optical-radar fusion excels."

"We are providing something the world has never had before — the ability to see through clouds with optical-grade clarity from space."

— GalaxEye Founders

The startup is part of a wave of Indian space companies that have emerged since India opened its space sector to private players in 2020. The Indian Space Research Organisation's legacy of low-cost, high-reliability missions laid the groundwork, but companies like GalaxEye, Skyroot Aerospace, and Agnikul Cosmos are now pushing into territory that ISRO never pursued commercially.

Defense and Commercial Applications

The OptoSAR technology has obvious defense applications. Military planners need imagery that works in monsoon conditions, at night, and through deliberate concealment — exactly the scenarios where optical-radar fusion excels. The Indian Armed Forces have been among the early interested parties, according to industry reports.

On the commercial side, agricultural monitoring, disaster response, urban planning, and insurance verification all stand to benefit. India's monsoon-dependent agriculture sector has long struggled with the limitations of optical-only satellite imagery, which fails precisely when flooding and crop damage are at their worst.

India's Private Space Moment

The launch comes weeks after Skyroot Aerospace made history with Vikram-1, India's first privately built orbital rocket. Together with Agnikul Cosmos's 3D-printed rocket engine tests and Pixxel's hyperspectral satellite constellation, Indian startups are establishing the country as a serious force in the global commercial space race.

For the diaspora, many of whom work in aerospace and technology sectors in the US and Europe, GalaxEye's achievement resonates as evidence that India's engineering talent can compete at the frontier. Several Indian-American venture capital firms and angel investors have backed the country's space startups, creating a bridge between Silicon Valley expertise and Indian innovation.

What's Next

GalaxEye plans to deploy a full constellation of OptoSAR satellites by 2028, aiming to provide near-real-time global coverage. The company is also exploring partnerships with international defense and intelligence agencies. With the payload now in orbit and collecting data, the next milestone will be demonstrating the technology's performance against established players like Planet Labs and Capella Space.
